title: Taiwan Isn’t Giving Up, It’s Pulling Apart
gist: Responding to the debate sparked by Simon Shuster's Atlantic piece on whether Taiwan will 'give up' under Chinese pressure, the author argues Taiwan is not surrendering but polarizing internally, and that trends over time in opinion, recruitment and defense spending matter more than snapshots.

insights.claim: Stated willingness to defend Taiwan in polls differs sharply from actual behavior under attack, and Taiwan is not a unitary actor, so single opinion snapshots are weak evidence of resolve.
insights.speaker: Dennis Lu-Chung Weng
insights.so_what: Investors pricing Taiwan risk should track trend data rather than headline polls.
insights.quote: telling a pollster “I would defend Taiwan” is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, and that Taiwan is not a unitary actor

insights.claim: The key metrics for judging Taiwan's resolve are trends over time in public opinion, military recruitment and defense spending.
insights.speaker: Dennis Lu-Chung Weng
insights.so_what: Defines observable indicators for monitoring cross-strait risk.
insights.quote: The question worth asking is how the trends in public opinion, military recruitment, defense spending and other metrics move over time, not what any single snapshot shows.

insights.claim: The author contends that Taiwan is not giving up in the face of Chinese pressure but is pulling apart through domestic polarization, exemplified by KMT-led opposition to the 2025 recalls.
insights.speaker: Dennis Lu-Chung Weng
insights.so_what: Internal division rather than capitulation could slow defense budgets and complicate deterrence, a subtler risk than outright surrender.
